e.t: This word means “indestructible”: it describes something that cannot be destroyed or brought to an end. It points to lasting permanence rather than something temporary, fragile, or subject to decay. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 7:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the quality of being incapable of destruction or ending.

e.t: This word means to contemplate something closely—to look carefully at it rather than give it only a passing glance. It describes attentive consideration or examination, whether directed toward something seen or toward its significance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts and Hebrews. Its basic idea is deliberate, focused attention: observing carefully and reflecting on what is being considered. The surrounding verse determines what is being examined and what response that careful attention calls for.

Resurrection means rising from the dead. It refers to the return of a dead person to life, and in the New Testament it is discussed as a real hope and future event. The word can describe resurrection generally, including the resurrection Jesus taught and the resurrection connected with the final raising of the dead. It occurs 42 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that resurrection is a recurring subject rather than a rare idea. Its precise significance in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

The word means “permanent”: lasting, enduring, and not temporary. It describes something that continues rather than passing away or changing quickly. This Greek New Testament word appears once, in Hebrews 7:24. Its basic sense is clear, but the exact way it applies in that verse must be understood from the surrounding sentence and passage. It expresses lasting continuance, not a brief or momentary condition.

e.t: This word means “disobey.” It describes the action of not obeying what has been commanded or required. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 14 times, so it refers to a recurring response rather than a rare or unusual idea. The word can describe people’s opposition to God’s will or their refusal to respond obediently. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

Redemption means being released or recovered from a condition of bondage, loss, or obligation. In the New Testament, it describes God’s saving work through Christ, including the forgiveness of sins and the promised completion of deliverance. The word appears 10 times in the Greek New Testament, often in connection with what believers receive through Christ and what they await from God. Its exact emphasis—present possession or future fulfillment—depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek New Testament word is a personal name, referring to “Asa” or “Asaph.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs two times in the Greek New Testament, both in Matthew 1:7–8. Since it is a name, its basic meaning is the person identified by that name; the surrounding verse supplies any further significance. “Asa” and “Asaph” are the two approved renderings associated with this name.

This word means “daybreak” or “daylight,” referring to the coming or presence of light after darkness. It describes the time when night gives way to day, or the light that marks daytime. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 20:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the arrival or presence of daylight rather than a person, action, or spiritual quality.

Gethsemane is a proper place-name, referring to a specific location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice: once in Matthew 26:36 and once in Mark 14:32. The English rendering preserves the name as “Gethsemane.” Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as the name of a place.

Gog is a name used for a particular figure, rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in Revelation 20:8, and the English translations retain it as “Gog.” The name itself does not provide a broader ordinary meaning; its precise significance comes from the surrounding passage, which identifies how the name is being used there.

e.h: To Tithe or Collect a Tenth
e.t: This word means “to collect a tenth” or “to tithe.” It refers to the act of taking or giving one part out of ten, expressed as a tenth portion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hebrews 7, where the wording concerns tithes. Thus, its basic sense is the practice of assigning or receiving a tenth, rather than a general word for giving or collecting. The precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “passed through,” “to go through,” or “to pass through.” It describes movement from one side, place, or point to another, emphasizing the act of going through an area or situation. It is a verb, so it tells what someone or something does rather than naming a person, place, or thing. The word occurs 43 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing especially often in Acts and Luke. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being crossed or traversed.

e.t: This word means “to come to one’s sense” or “to wake up.” It functions as a verb, describing a call to regain clear judgment and alertness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 15:34. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context. Its central idea remains a summons to become alert rather than continue in an unaware or confused state.

Elisha is the personal name represented by this Greek New Testament word. It identifies Elisha rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 4:27, and its English rendering is “Elisha.” As a proper name, it functions chiefly to identify the person named, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular context.

This word refers to a market or marketplace—a public place connected with buying, selling, and trade. Its meaning can include the commercial activity associated with such a place, not merely the physical location. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 2:16, and is rendered “marketplace.” The word therefore identifies a setting where commerce takes place. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a marketplace or place of trade.

e.t: This word means “to hear” or “to listen to,” describing the act of receiving and paying attention to what is spoken. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 6:2. The surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise force of the action there, but the basic sense remains hearing or listening to a spoken message.

Esli is a personal name preserved as “Esli” in English. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 3:25. The word identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or general concept. Its significance in that verse is best understood from the surrounding passage and the person being named, rather than by assigning it an additional meaning not given here.

This word means “another,” “other,” or “others,” referring to a person or thing distinct from the one already mentioned. It can identify someone else, a different group, or additional people or things, depending on the sentence. As an adjective or pronoun, it helps distinguish one person or thing from another without, by itself, expressing whether the difference is good or bad. It occurs 98 times in the Greek New Testament, so its exact force is determined by the surrounding wording and context.

This word means “divine,” describing what belongs to, comes from, or is associated with God. It functions as a describing word, marking something as having a God-related character rather than an ordinary human one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: once in Acts and twice in 2 Peter. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a direct reference to what is divine.

e.t: This word means “to quarrel,” describing the act of arguing or engaging in a dispute. It is a verb, so it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, making it a rare word in that corpus. Its precise force in that occurrence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a hostile disagreement or verbal conflict.

Jesse is a personal name referring to the father of David. In the Greek New Testament, it identifies Jesse in genealogical records and in passages that speak of David’s family line. The name occurs five times, appearing in Matthew, Luke, Acts, and Romans. It is therefore not a general description or title, but a specific name used to identify the person Jesse within the biblical account.

This word means “Judaism,” referring to the Jewish religious identity and way of life. It names the religious system or commitment associated with being Jewish, rather than describing a single action or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, and both occurrences are in Galatians 1:13–14. Its precise force in either sentence depends on the surrounding verse context, but its central sense remains Judaism.

This word means “speck,” referring to a very small particle or bit. It is a noun used in the Greek New Testament six times, all in Matthew and Luke. Its ordinary sense is something tiny and noticeable, especially when contrasted with something much larger. The word appears in five verses, including Matthew 7:3–5 and Luke 6:41–42. The surrounding context determines the particular point being made with this small object.

e.t: This word means “to lock up,” describing the act of confining someone or keeping someone shut in. It focuses on the physical action of placing a person in secure confinement, rather than on the reason for doing so or the person’s feelings. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Luke and once in Acts, showing this specific action in two separate passages. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “to be sealed up” or “to seal.” It describes something closed or secured with a seal, indicating that access or opening has been restricted. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 5:1. The word itself expresses the act or condition of sealing, while the surrounding verse determines what has been sealed and why that matters. Its basic idea is firm closure or secure restriction, rather than merely covering or shutting something casually.

This word means a harp, a stringed musical instrument. It is a noun naming the instrument itself, whether one harp or several harps are being mentioned. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times: once in 1 Corinthians and three times in Revelation. Its references connect the instrument with musical sound and worship, but the word itself identifies the harp rather than describing a particular song, person, or spiritual lesson. The surrounding verse and passage determine how the harp functions in each occurrence.

This word means “raven,” referring to the dark-feathered bird. It is a concrete noun naming a particular kind of bird rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 12:24. The word itself identifies the bird; the surrounding verse and passage determine what is being said about it there. Its meaning is therefore straightforward and specific: a raven, a bird named as part of the natural world.

e.t: This word means “to judge” or “to decide.” It describes assessing a matter, reaching a verdict, or determining what is right. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to a person judging others, people being judged, or a decision that will be made. It is used 114 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages about judging rightly and about future judgment. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Levi is a personal name, referring to a man or to the Israelite tribe descended from him. In the Greek New Testament, it is consistently rendered “Levi,” so it functions as a proper name rather than a descriptive title or ordinary vocabulary word. The name occurs eight times in the New Testament, including references to individuals in the genealogies and to Levi who was called by Jesus. It also refers to the tribe in Hebrews and Revelation. Its precise identity in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “drunkenness,” referring to the condition of being drunk. It names a state caused by excessive drinking rather than a single act or moment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: once each in Luke, Romans, and Galatians. These occurrences place the word among behaviors warned against or treated as spiritually dangerous, but the word itself primarily identifies drunkenness as a condition. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Moses is the personal name of the man known in the Bible as Moses. In the Greek New Testament, this word refers to him by name rather than describing a general quality or action. It appears 80 times across 79 New Testament verses, showing that Moses remains a significant person in the New Testament’s references to Israel’s history, law, and testimony. The word first appears in Matthew 8:4 and last appears in Revelation 15:3. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This word describes someone or something foreign or strange—outside what is familiar or normally expected. It can refer to people regarded as outsiders, or to something perceived as unfamiliar. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times across 14 verses, showing that this idea appears in several kinds of statements. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central sense remains the unfamiliar or foreign character of the person or thing described.

This word means “bone” or “bones,” referring to the hard parts forming the framework of the body. It is a noun used for individual bones or bones considered together. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, and each occurrence is rendered with one of these two closely related forms. The word appears in passages addressing the body’s physical structure, so its basic meaning remains concrete rather than symbolic by itself. The surrounding context determines whether the reference concerns one bone or several bones.

Patmos is a place name, referring to a specific location rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Revelation 1:9, and the English rendering is “Patmos.” Because the available wording identifies the place but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its precise significance in that passage must be understood from the wider context.

This word means “clay,” “mud,” or “of clay.” It refers to soft, earthy material that can be handled or formed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times: five occurrences are in John and one is in Romans. Its central meaning remains the same in each occurrence—a substance made from earth, whether described as clay or mud in English translations.

This word means “citizenship,” referring to a person’s civic belonging or status as a citizen. It names the community or realm to which someone belongs, rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Philippians 3:20. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to citizenship and the belonging that citizenship expresses.

This word refers to an older woman or old woman. It is a specific description of a female person who is advanced in age, rather than a general word for any woman. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 2:3. Its exact role in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but the word itself identifies the person as an older woman. The central meaning remains straightforward: a woman who is older in years.

Rachel is a personal name referring to Rachel, the woman named in Matthew 2:18. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, and its meaning is straightforward because it identifies a specific person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name connects Matthew’s quotation with Rachel known from the Old Testament, while the precise force of the reference belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. As a name, it functions as a proper noun and is not normally translated into a different descriptive meaning.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “farewell” and “to be strong.” It is a parting expression that can convey the wish that someone remain well, steady, or strong as they go. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 15:29. Its basic sense is therefore a closing greeting or farewell rather than a description of an object, person, or action repeated throughout the New Testament.

The word means “humble” or “lowly,” describing a person or condition marked by humility rather than elevation or self-importance. It characterizes someone who is not seeking a high position, or someone regarded as lowly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages in Matthew, Luke, Romans, 2 Corinthians, James, and 1 Peter. Its central idea is humility or lowliness, while the surrounding sentence determines its precise force.

This word means “four,” identifying a quantity of four people, things, directions, or other counted items. It functions as a number word and can describe how many there are or how something is divided or arranged. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 41 times, including descriptions of four winds, four parts, and four living creatures. Its specific reference—whether to people, objects, or directions—comes from the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: “Tyrian” refers to a person from Tyre, the Phoenician city. It functions as a descriptive name for people associated with that place rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Acts 12:20. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning identifies someone as Tyrian—that is, connected with Tyre.

This word means “meeting,” referring to an encounter in which people come together. It describes the act or occasion of going out to meet someone, rather than a person or place itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each in a different verse, so its precise force depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic idea remains a meeting: people moving toward one another or gathering together.

This word means “philosophy,” referring to a system of thought or wisdom that people follow. It is a noun used once in the Greek New Testament, in Colossians 2:8. The word itself identifies philosophy as a kind of teaching or intellectual outlook, while the surrounding passage is needed to understand how that particular use applies. Its central meaning remains a humanly developed way of thinking or pursuing wisdom.

This word means “natural,” describing what belongs to nature, follows natural origin, or has the character of what is natural. It functions as an adjective, so it identifies a person, thing, or action in relation to nature rather than presenting a separate action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Romans and 2 Peter. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This word refers to a false teacher—someone presented as a teacher whose teaching is false. It is a plural noun, so it can describe more than one such teacher. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Peter 2:1. The basic meaning identifies the person by the character of the teaching: these are teachers associated with falsehood rather than truth. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what those teachers did in that verse.

e.t: This word means “to assemble” or “to assemble together”—to bring people into one gathered group. It emphasizes coming together rather than remaining separated. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Luke 24:33. The word’s basic sense is straightforward: people are gathered together in one place or community. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a collective assembling.
